title: Notice Red-Team and Pleading Triage for Landlords
one_liner: An adversarial checker that tries to break every eviction notice before it is served, then triages incoming AI-drafted pleadings and prices cash-for-keys exits.
customer: Mid-size operators (500-10,000 units) and the landlord-tenant law firms that serve them on flat-fee matters.
problem: Federal pro se filings topped 41,000 in 2025 against a 23,000 average for 2005-2022, and one tenant filed 22 pleadings in a weekend. Operators pay outside counsel to triage each one while units sit idle, and some conclude cash-for-keys is cheaper than winning. Tenants' AI can find a defective notice in minutes, so procedural errors are now fatal.
solution: An adversarial reviewer checks each notice (cure periods, statutory language, service method, ledger accuracy including banned fees) against jurisdiction rules before service. Inbound pleadings are classified, deadlines docketed, and a 48-hour decision brief compares cost-to-contest with a benchmarked cash-for-keys offer that respects relocation rules. An evidence pack (ledger, communications, inspection logs) is auto-assembled. Licensed attorneys supervise, to avoid unauthorized-practice risk.
why_now: Generative tools have made pro se filings cheap and voluminous, and operators are shrinking staff and leaning on AI leasing, so their record-keeping is thin. Municipal fee bans add new ways a ledger can be wrong.
revenue_model: $3-6 per unit per year platform fee plus $75-250 per triaged matter; law-firm seats at $300-600 per month.
non_obvious_insight: The real cost is not the pleading but the vacant unit while it sits in dispute, so the winning metric is decision speed inside 48 hours. Both sides are now AI-armed, and the defensible edge is an adversarial 'red team' that finds your process defects before the tenant does.
first_30_days: Partner with two landlord-tenant firms in a high-volume market. Build a notice checker for two jurisdictions and run it free on 200 historical notices to show catch-rates. Convert firms to a $500 per month seat and operators to a per-matter fee.

title: Market Rulebook Red Team for New Venues
one_liner: Turn a trading venue's plain-English rulebook into an executable model, then use adversarial agents to find manipulation exploits and propose rule patches before real attackers do.
customer: Operators of new or small marketplaces: CFTC-registered event-contract and prediction-market venues, tokenized-asset and crypto exchanges, carbon-credit registries, energy and capacity market operators, GPU-compute spot exchanges, and ad-auction platforms.
problem: Modern electronic markets are built for speed and transparency, which has 'created new attack surfaces and systemic risks', and they 'can be manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'. Venues test their matching engine software, but nobody systematically tests the market rules themselves (settlement sources, auction tie-breaks, position limits, fee rebates) for exploits. Regulators expect venues to show their contracts and rules resist manipulation, but there is no standard way to prove it.
solution: An agent pipeline. Step 1: an LLM converts the rulebook or tariff PDF into a formal mechanism spec (order types, matching rules, settlement, fees). Step 2: an agent-based simulator with attacker agents searches for profitable manipulation strategies (wash trading, spoofing and layering, oracle or settlement-source attacks, self-dealing through fee rebates, cross-market squeezes). Step 3: it proposes rule patches and re-runs the attacks as regression tests. Deliver a fuzz report and a CI-style re-run whenever the rules change.
why_now: DARPA's Intrinsic Market Resilience (IMR) program, with a proposers day October 1, 2026, abstracts due October 22 and proposals due December 7, 2026, explicitly bets that LLM automation plus rigorous modeling can automatically model market designs, find weaknesses and recommend repairs. New event-contract, tokenized and compute markets are launching faster than their rulebooks can be reviewed. LLMs only recently became good enough at turning long legal text into formal specs.
revenue_model: $25k to $60k fixed-price rulebook audit. $3k to $8k per month for continuous re-testing when rules or fee schedules change. Possible subcontract or teaming revenue on DARPA IMR or follow-on federal work.
non_obvious_insight: A rulebook is code that nobody compiles. DARPA is paying to build the compiler-plus-fuzzer, and the same tool works on any venue, so the government-funded R&D is a free market validation of the product category. The IMR page states the problem ('manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'), names markets from 'equities and bonds to energy and cloud computing resources', and describes the LLM-plus-formal-modeling approach: https://www.darpa.mil/research/programs/intrinsic-market-resilience-imr. Caveat: the public page names no specific exploits and says nothing about commercial adoption, so the private-sector demand (for example the CFTC's requirement that contracts not be readily susceptible to manipulation) is my inference from background knowledge, not from the DARPA page.
first_30_days: Pick 3 public rulebooks or tariffs (a new prediction-market venue, a public energy market tariff, a carbon registry methodology). Run the pipeline and publish 3 short teardown posts showing a concrete exploit and a patch. Email the compliance and product heads of 30 newly launched venues with their own teardown. Sell 2 fixed-price audits at $25k. In parallel, submit an abstract by October 22 or offer teaming to IMR prime bidders.

title: Inherited-Rental Stabilization Service for Estate Attorneys
one_liner: A flat-fee 30-day service that stabilizes rental properties the moment an owner dies, sold through probate attorneys and trust officers who fear personal liability.
customer: Probate and trust-and-estates attorneys, professional fiduciaries and bank trust departments who represent executors and heirs of deceased small landlords. Attorney or fiduciary pays the flat fee out of the estate. Beneficiaries later pay ongoing management or sale-prep fees.
problem: The average small landlord is in their 60s or older, and a wave of these owners is dying and passing on 2-to-30-unit portfolios to heirs who have never landlorded. In the first 60 to 90 days after death everything degrades. Tenants get confused about who to pay and some quietly stop, so collections drop 20 to 40%. The named insured on the policy is dead and coverage gets contested or non-renewed. Security deposits, a legal liability that has to be accounted for in trust, are mingled into the deceased's personal account. Leases are undocumented handshake month-to-months, and vendors stop being paid. The attorney does not want to run a rental business but is exposed to a beneficiary surcharge claim if value leaks.
solution: A productized 'Day-1 Stabilization Package' delivered by a small field team and software. It has five parts. First, a tenant estoppel and 'pay here' notice with a new rent-collection account, sent within 5 days. Second, a rent-roll and lease audit, verifying every tenant, deposit and lease term against bank records. Third, deposit-liability reconciliation and a segregated trust account. Fourth, insurance re-papering: new named-insured and vacancy status filings. Fifth, a code-compliance and deferred-maintenance walk-through, with photos, for the estate inventory and stepped-up-basis appraisal support. The output is a court-ready fiduciary report the attorney can file. The last step is an option: convert to ongoing management at a preferential rate, or a sale-ready package for listing.
why_now: The great wealth transfer from boomers is reaching real estate now, and small individual landlords are among the oldest owner cohorts. Rising property values make each estate's rental portfolio high-stakes. Attorneys are reluctant to run operating businesses, and fiduciary surcharge risk is well understood. Large PM firms ignore 6-unit estates. Cloud rent collection and e-sign tools make a 30-day remote-plus-local process feasible for a tiny team.
revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,000 flat fee per estate (scaled by unit count), paid by the estate. About 30 to 40% of estates convert into ongoing management at 7 to 9% of rent, or into a listing or sale referral with a 1 to 2% fee. Bank trust departments can be sold an annual retainer.
non_obvious_insight: The best property-management clients are never won through marketing. They arrive through a death, and the person deciding who gets the call is an attorney who cares about liability, not price or software features. The attorney's real product need is documentation to defend against beneficiary surcharge claims, not better rent collection. The real revenue leak in the first 90 days is the 'ghost landlord' period, when tenants do not know who to pay.
first_30_days: Write the checklist and notice templates (a weekend of work if you have PM experience). Contact 30 probate attorneys and 5 corporate fiduciary or trust officers in one metro, offering a free 45-minute CLE-style talk on 'the first 90 days of an inherited rental portfolio' through the county bar's trusts and estates section. Offer a discounted first stabilization at cost to two attorneys for testimonials and case studies. Line up a bookkeeper and a local handyman for the field-work side and use existing PM software for rent collection.

title: Good-Better-Best Estimate Engine for Vet Clinics
one_liner: AI scribes are turning into a free feature, so the money moves to the moment a client sees the estimate: automate tiered spectrum-of-care plans that turn declines into partial acceptance.
customer: Emergency/urgent-care hospitals and 2-10 DVM independent general practices, where estimates over $1,000 are routine. Buyer is the practice owner or hospital manager.
problem: Per the briefing, 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 86% alter treatment plans weekly for financial reasons. Estimates are still hand-built as one gold-standard plan, so declines are lost revenue and a source of moral distress (33% of vets find below-gold care distressing). Nobody logs why clients decline.
solution: Reads the diagnosis or SOAP note from any scribe or PIMS and drafts three clinician-approved tiers: full workup, stabilize-and-monitor, and essential/palliative. Each tier is priced from the clinic's own fee schedule, with consent language, expected-outcome ranges and stage-gated steps (approve step 1 now, decide step 2 after results). Financing and insurance pre-check sit on the same screen. Every decline reason is captured and feeds a protocol library written with boarded clinicians. Ships as a browser overlay on the PIMS estimate screen.
why_now: IDEXX bought the CoVet AI scribe on 2026-09-16 and says it will stay compatible with non-IDEXX systems. That marks documentation AI as a bundled strategic feature and squeezes standalone scribes. Clinic visits have reportedly fallen three years running, and price, not demand, is the constraint.
revenue_model: SaaS at $300-600 per clinic per month, plus an optional success fee of 3-5% of incremental accepted revenue measured against a pre-pilot baseline. Later, anonymized decline-reason data sold to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders think the AI prize is saving doctors' time on notes. The budget line is revenue at the decision moment, and the scribe is just a commodity input to it. The decline reason is a dataset nobody collects, and it is what financiers and insurers most want.
first_30_days: Sign 5 ER/urgent-care sites and 5 independents. Take each site's last 20 de-identified declined estimates, have a contract boarded vet rebuild them as three-tier plans, and run a 4-week pilot tracking acceptance rate. Charge a $1,500 pilot fee. Prototype the browser overlay with an LLM plus the clinic's fee-schedule export.

title: Independent Gauntlet for Police and Counter-Drone Buyers
one_liner: A buyer-funded, video-first test lab that flies and publishes open-protocol results on police first-responder drones and counter-drone detection, the way the Pentagon's public Gauntlets do for its own buyers, funded by agency subscriptions and never by vendors.
customer: Police, fire and emergency-management tech buyers at city and county agencies ($1,200-3,000 per agency-year for full data, vendor scorecards and RFP language), buyer consortia, and grant-funded counter-UAS programs (FEMA's $500M program, Dallas's $10M set-aside).
problem: Local buyers cannot audit vendors: state and local tech contracts average 7 years, only 5.3% of AI-relevant provisions address transparency, and GenAI-written RFPs make every proposal look perfect. Vendor claims are unreliable: only 24% of drones reached 10 km in the Pentagon's Gauntlet 1, Cape Canaveral's radars miss quadcopters, and 700+ drones were seized around one World Cup stadium. Trade media and cooperative marketplaces are vendor-funded, so independent performance data does not exist.
solution: Quarterly standardized tests covering range, wind, latency, false alarms against birds and RF clutter, and detection of cooperative test drones only (no jamming). Runs are recorded with signed telemetry and raw video so results cannot be disputed or edited, and protocols are open. Drone creators co-host as pilots and distribute the long-form video, while agencies pay for data, scorecards, sample RFP language and an ask-us desk. Vendors may buy re-tests only after results are public.
why_now: The Pentagon's public Gauntlets (Gauntlet 2 in Sept 2026: 23 platforms, 19 companies, 1,858 sorties) normalized head-to-head public testing. Counter-drone money is flowing to cities, sponsored and AI-written content swamps review media, and local surveillance-tech purchases now face public scrutiny.
revenue_model: Agency subscriptions, custom pre-procurement tests paid from grants, and paid training. No vendor sponsorship, which is the trust asset.
non_obvious_insight: DoD's Gauntlet works because the buyer controls the test. Local agencies have the same need but no lab budget, and the creator-media model (audience-funded, no sponsors) is exactly the structure that makes an independent lab self-sustaining. Vendor-funded trade media and vendor-listing marketplaces are structurally unable to be the referee.
first_30_days: Buy five sub-$5K first-responder-class drones and run one head-to-head on range, wind and latency, then publish it. Email 200 police tech sergeants and drone-as-first-responder coordinators and sign 10 agency subscriptions at $1,200. File public-records requests for existing agency test data to seed the second episode.

title: Hallmark-Style Microdramas for Women 45+
one_liner: A genre studio making 60-episode vertical dramas (cozy mystery, faith-and-family, second-act romance) for the older female audience the romance-and-revenge apps under-serve, sold through web checkout.
customer: Women aged 40-65 in the US, UK, Canada and Australia paying via coin packs or weekly subscriptions. Aggregator apps such as ReelShort and DramaBox are a second customer as licensees.
problem: Microdramas are a roughly $11B global market, with about $1.3B a year of US spend, mostly women 30-60. Supply skews toward billionaire-romance, werewolf and revenge tropes. Genres this audience already pays for on Hallmark, Lifetime and faith networks are thin.
solution: Shoot 60-70 episode series for $50-90k on 8-day schedules with real actors, and use AI only in post (subtitles, cleanup, ADR), not for performers. Test three genres with $3k of Meta ads per pilot, license winners to aggregators for minimum guarantees, then push loyal viewers to your own web-checkout app.
why_now: Epic's April 2025 ruling stopped Apple charging fees on purchases made outside its store in the US, so a vertical-drama app can keep most of the margin on web checkout. Series cycle times are under two weeks, and the market has proven willingness to pay.
revenue_model: Coin and subscription revenue via own app (LTV-driven), plus aggregator licensing fees and minimum guarantees, plus brand integrations.
non_obvious_insight: The leaders optimized for early-adopter tropes. Viewers 45+ already pay for TV subscriptions, have cards on file, are cheap to reach on Facebook, and churn less. Scarcity of content for them is a supply gap, not a demand gap.
first_30_days: Shoot a 10-episode pilot for about $12k. Run a $3k ad test on three genres and pick the winner by cost per paying viewer. Pitch two aggregators for a minimum guarantee, and stand up a web paywall using an off-the-shelf subscription funnel tool.

title: Unstaffed Overnight ICU for Vet Clinics
one_liner: Radar-based contactless vitals and camera analytics let general practices keep IV-fluid and post-op patients overnight without a 24-hour staff, easing ER transfers and ER overload.
customer: 2-10 DVM general practices and low-cost clinics with a small treatment ward, plus shelter medical wards such as parvo units.
problem: With about 2 techs per vet, most clinics cannot staff nights, so hospitalized pets are transferred to 24-hour ERs at higher cost, sent home early or not treated. That drives owner cost, client loss and ER crowding.
solution: A low-cost mmWave radar puck per cage measures respiratory rate and motion, with a camera to watch IV lines and pumps. An on-site alert plus a pooled remote overnight RVT/DVM desk cover 20 clinics, with thresholds tuned by species and weight.
why_now: Consumer sleep-tracking made mmWave sensors cheap, edge vision models run on small devices, the tech shortage is structural, and the spectrum-of-care movement wants intermediate options between full transfer and no treatment.
revenue_model: $150 per cage hardware plus $79-149 per cage per month, and per-night remote-coverage fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone tries to automate diagnosis. The binding constraint is night hours: the lack of an awake person forces a general practice to hand revenue and clients to the ER. Monitoring substitutes for staying awake, not for the doctor.
first_30_days: Buy off-the-shelf radar and cameras and instrument 4 cages in 2 friendly clinics. Log respiratory-rate accuracy against manual counts for 30 nights. Sell $99-per-cage pilots and recruit pooled overnight RVT coverage.

title: Mahjong Leagues for Senior Living Communities
one_liner: A turnkey mahjong program (kits, instructors, scoring app, inter-community leagues) sold to senior-living activity directors.
customer: Activity directors at independent and assisted living communities (roughly 30k in the US), 55+ HOAs, and library systems.
problem: Mahjong is booming: CNN (19 Sept 2026) covers the explosion, Yelp searches for mahjong clubs rose about 4,467% in 2025, and the National Mah Jongg League reports 350k+ members. Coverage frames it as a Gen Z and millennial aesthetic trend. Meanwhile senior-living calendars need social, cognitive, low-injury weekly activities, and American mahjong is hard to learn and hard to staff with teachers.
solution: A subscription with a 4-table starter kit, certified instructor visits (in person or video), monthly inter-community league nights with a shared leaderboard and trophy, a coordinator app, and staff training so the community can run it alone.
why_now: The mainstream boom is producing demand and a supply of instructors from the new club scene. Pickleball injuries make low-impact alternatives attractive for the same age group.
revenue_model: $300-600/month per community, $250 kits, per-visit instructor fees, and tile-maker sponsorships.
non_obvious_insight: Tile brands and influencers chase young buyers with $200 designer sets. The recurring money sits with older players who play weekly and with institutions that have a budget line called 'activities'. Inter-facility leagues create retention and sales compounding, because a community that joins forces its rivals to join.
first_30_days: Approach 20 senior communities in one metro via activity-director networks. Run free two-week pilots staffed by 2 volunteer instructors recruited from local clubs. Convert 5 into $300/month accounts and stage the first inter-community match.

title: Roof Rebuttal Kits for Aerial-Photo Insurance Drops
one_liner: A 48-hour, flat-fee evidence packet and cheap-fix dispatch that lets homeowners beat insurer non-renewals based on aerial imagery instead of paying $20k for an unneeded roof.
customer: Homeowners who receive a non-renewal or 'replace your roof in 30-60 days' letter (paying $249-$399 flat). The hidden second buyer is independent insurance agents, who lose the commission when a policy leaves and would pay a white-label subscription.
problem: Carriers and their imagery vendors (State Farm reportedly uses CAPE Analytics and Nearmap) flag moss, algae, skylights, solar panels, tree overhang, pools or trampolines from aerial photos. Homeowners get a short cure window, are told to replace a roof (one Santa Ana homeowner was quoted about $20,000 with a May 1 deadline and could not find replacement coverage), and are often refused the images. In one Galveston case the roofer said the roof only needed a thorough cleaning, yet the insurer would not share its report or photos.
solution: Local dispatch of a licensed roof inspector or drone pilot who produces an insurer-formatted rebuttal packet: dated, geotagged photos, remaining-life certification, an overlay labeling the skylight, solar panel or moss that the insurer's image mislabeled, and a written cure quote. Where a real defect exists, a vetted soft-wash or repair contractor does the cheap cure (hundreds of dollars, not replacement). The kit also includes a request-the-images letter, a state Department of Insurance complaint draft, and a re-shop packet showing roof condition to alternative carriers.
why_now: Aerial and AI underwriting went mainstream in 2024-2026. DroneXL (Mar 2026) reports imagery-driven drops nationwide and that Texas non-renewals nearly doubled from 2020 to 2023. California proposed insurer-notification rules in 2025, and Massachusetts proposed a right to view the images. Consumers now need a fast, standard counter-evidence format, and cheap drones and inspection apps make a 48-hour turnaround affordable.
revenue_model: $249-$399 per packet, plus a 10-20% referral fee from cleaning and roofing contractors on cure jobs, plus a $99-$199/month white-label plan for independent agents who send at-risk clients.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is an evidence-format problem, not an insurance problem, and the cure often costs 2-5% of the replacement. A San Francisco couple insured for about 50 years had a Liberty Mutual non-renewal reversed within an hour of media pressure after a licensed roofer's written, photographed inspection showed about 20 years of remaining life (https://www.aol.com/finance/insurer-dropped-san-francisco-homeowners-131500464.html). Most homeowners cannot get that leverage. DroneXL documents the $20k quote, the Galveston 'cleaning only' case, and the vendor names (https://dronexl.co/2026/03/11/insurance-drone-roof-inspections/). United Policyholders confirms that correcting misidentifications with photos works and that only about 30 days' notice is typical (https://uphelp.org/aerial-photos-are-leading-to-insurance-non-renewals/). Reddit itself was unreachable from this environment, so this demand evidence comes from press and advocate sources describing the same recurring r/homeowners situation.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with heavy non-renewals (Houston/Galveston, the Bay Area, or the Colorado Front Range). Sign two soft-wash companies and one roof inspector with a drone at about $150 per inspection, and build a one-page site aimed at searches like 'State Farm non-renewal roof'. Post in neighborhood groups, offer the packet to 10 independent agents, and run the first 20-30 packets at $299, tracking reversal rate to build a public success statistic.

title: Right-Size Rx: Deprescribing After GLP-1 Starts
one_liner: Pharmacist outreach that adjusts insulin, sulfonylureas and BP meds in the weeks after a GLP-1 start, sold to payers on avoided harm and drug spend.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid MCOs, ACOs and self-funded employers with large diabetic and hypertensive populations.
problem: Tirzepatide trial protocols recommend cutting sulfonylureas by at least 50% and basal insulin by at least 20% at start, because GLP-1 weight loss lowers glucose and blood pressure. In real practice nobody is triggered or paid to do this, so patients face hypoglycemia, hypotension and falls, while brand diabetes drugs (SGLT2s, DPP-4s) keep getting refilled.
solution: Claims-triggered (and pharmacy-partner-triggered for cash-pay fills) pharmacist outreach at days 7-28 after first fill among patients on insulin, SU or antihypertensives. Collaborative-practice protocols to adjust or recommend changes, home BP and CGM review, and a savings and safety ledger for the payer.
why_now: The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge started Jul 1, 2026 and cash pills at $149-$299 are pushing GLP-1s into older, more medicated patients. Payers are fixated on the GLP-1 price line and are missing the neighboring drug lines.
revenue_model: $2-4 per targeted member per month, or $250 per completed episode, plus a share of measurable avoided ED visits and drug savings.
non_obvious_insight: The near-term safety and cost of GLP-1s sits in the other drugs on the patient's list. Payers can offset part of the GLP-1 cost by trimming those, so it belongs on a CFO's line item, not just a quality dashboard.
first_30_days: Approach one regional MA plan or IPA and one pharmacist group. Run a 90-day pilot on 300 patients identified from Rx claims. Measure interventions made, hypoglycemia events and avoided fills, and hand back a savings ledger.

title: Dye-Free SKU Sprints for Walmart Suppliers
one_liner: Fixed-price, eight-week reformulation sprints with pooled colorant supply for mid-size suppliers facing dye deadlines.
customer: Mid-size co-manufacturers, private-label suppliers and regional bakers and candy makers without in-house R&D.
problem: Walmart private label goes dye-free in January 2027 and FDA targets petroleum dye phase-out by December 2027, while reformulation costs $50k-500k per SKU and takes 12-24+ months to validate.
solution: Per-SKU-family sprints covering color matching, stability and shelf-life testing, and access to a pooled natural-colorant supply contract for annatto, butterfly pea and similar inputs.
why_now: Products with FD&C dyes are about 4% of items but $57.8B in sales, natural colorant demand is projected to rise 400-500%, and the US is 98% import-dependent for annatto.
revenue_model: $25-60k per SKU family plus margin on pooled colorant supply.
non_obvious_insight: Validation is the bottleneck rather than ideas. A shared test lab and pooled purchasing let mid-size firms without R&D meet the deadline that big brands will already have met.
first_30_days: Interview 20 private-label suppliers to Walmart, offer a discounted first sprint to three, and line up one colorant supplier and one contract lab.

title: EU Liable-Party-of-Record for AI Products
one_liner: The registered agent of the AI era: an insured EU entity that stands as authorised representative under the new Product Liability Directive and keeps clients' evidence court-ready.
customer: Non-EU makers (10-200 staff) of AI-enabled consumer hardware and apps, such as robot vacuums, wearables, AI toys, smart-home and e-mobility firmware, selling into the EU via Amazon, Shopify or retailers.
problem: From 9 Dec 2026 software and AI count as 'products' under Directive 2024/2853. Courts can order disclosure of evidence, a defendant who stonewalls faces a presumption of defect, and liability cascades to importers, authorised representatives and fulfilment providers when no EU manufacturer exists. Small non-EU firms have no solvent EU counterparty, no organised technical file, and no cover. Marketplaces and logistics partners will start demanding all three.
solution: A fixed-fee service with four parts. (1) An EU entity acting as authorised representative and liable operator of record. (2) A 'disclosure-ready dossier': model and version registry, safety case, incident and OTA-update logs, and retention rules, collected through simple exports so a court order can be met in days. (3) EU-language complaint and defect intake plus recall coordination. (4) A bundled PLD policy through a fronting carrier or MGA, priced lower because the dossier removes unknowns.
why_now: The transposition deadline is 9 Dec 2026, about ten weeks away, and products placed on the market after it fall under the new regime. Only a minority of member states have finished transposing, so uncertainty peaks now. The December 2024 GPSR rule created a wave of paid 'EU responsible person' services, which shows small sellers buy this kind of compliance. Carriers filing broad AI exclusions (AIG, Berkley, Great American, ISO CG 40 47/48) push AI firms toward affirmative cover.
revenue_model: $1.5k-6k per month per client by risk tier, a $5-15k onboarding fee for the dossier, 10-15% commission on the bundled policy, and incident-response retainers. 40 clients at about $3k per month is roughly $1.4M ARR.
non_obvious_insight: The PLD creates an evidence-access war (disclosure orders plus presumptions of defect), and small firms lose it by default because they cannot produce coherent records. What clients buy is not legal advice but a solvent, present EU party who can hand a court a clean file. Demand will arrive through the distribution chain first, because retailers and marketplaces will impose it by contract before any regulator enforces it.
first_30_days: Partner with an EU product-liability law firm (NL, IE or DE) for the entity and an opinion letter. Publish a 10-page 'PLD readiness for AI hardware' guide. Pitch it to GPSR-rep leads, hardware accelerator alumni and Amazon/Shopify hardware sellers. Sign 5 founding clients at $1k per month. Get one European MGA or Lloyd's coverholder to quote the bundled policy.

title: Gig Social-Security Compliance Engine for Mid-Size Platforms
one_liner: A four-week compliance package for India's long tail of aggregator platforms that cannot build labour-code tooling in-house.
customer: Indian home-services, logistics, ride and staffing platforms with 5k-100k gig workers.
problem: India's labour codes require aggregator contributions to a social security fund and worker registration. Over 20% of gig workers log 70+ hours a week, and the government forced platforms to drop 10-minute branding in Jan 2026. Founders bear the audit exposure.
solution: e-Shram registration sync, contribution computation, hours-worked flags and worker benefit statements. The wedge is a fixed-fee readiness audit and setup for logistics and home-service platforms.
why_now: Labour codes are now in force, enforcement is starting, and quick-commerce attrition (51% at Zepto) pushes platforms to show worker-welfare records.
revenue_model: Rs 10-30 per worker per month plus a setup fee.
non_obvious_insight: Large platforms build in-house. The 500 mid-size platforms cannot, and they have real budgets because penalties land on founders.
first_30_days: Run free readiness audits for 10 platforms and refine the contribution calculation with a labour-law firm partner.

title: Data Estate Broker for Main Street Closures
one_liner: An appraisal-and-brokerage service that finds, de-identifies and sells the operational exhaust (quotes, work orders, dispatch logs, inspection records) of retiring or closing non-tech firms to AI buyers.
customer: Owners, business brokers, insolvency practitioners and CPAs handling closures of small manufacturers, freight brokers, insurance agencies, energy contractors and engineering firms. The buyers are vertical-AI startups and labs that need real workflow data.
problem: Failed-company data is now valuable. Google bought bankrupt Spirit Airlines' data for $10M: 100M emails, 30M+ recorded calls, 763,000+ flights of ops data, 1.2M fuel slips and 787,452 parts purchases. Mercor was the underbidder. But SimpleClosure, the main shutdown broker, only serves VC-backed startups, whose H1 2026 shutdowns were 27.3% B2B SaaS and 14.4% AI. Buyers say they want scarce data from manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services and logistics. Those firms close or retire constantly and have nobody to appraise or sell their data.
solution: Start with operational, non-consumer-PII data, which is the least legally fraught. Examples are work orders, quotes and bids, dispatch and routing logs, inspection and maintenance records, CAD revision histories, and internal Q&A threads. Run a 'data asset scan' ($500-1,500, credited against fees), then rights review and de-identification. Package the results as licensed corpora, run a sealed-bid sale to vertical-AI buyers and take a 25-35% success fee. Recruit business brokers, liquidators and trade associations as referral partners. Consumer call recordings and customer emails are excluded until counsel signs off.
why_now: Buyers proved a price in Aug 2026 (Spirit, $10M) and there is a losing bidder waiting. SimpleClosure's own asset report shows buyers paying tens to hundreds of thousands for unique corpora and wanting 'how real work actually got done.' Vertical AI agents for trades and logistics need training data that does not exist on the open web. Small-business retirements are a multi-year wave, and Sherline Tools going out of business (Sept 2026) is one example.
revenue_model: 25-35% success fee on data licence sales, plus a $500-1,500 appraisal fee credited against it. Optional recurring 'living licence' fees for firms that stay open.
non_obvious_insight: The market for dead-company data exists, but the only broker is aimed at software startups, while buyers explicitly want boring industries. Evidence: Google's $10M Spirit purchase with Mercor as underbidder (https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/18/google-buys-crashed-airline-spirits-data-at-auction-because-ai/5288962). The HN discussion notes that Scale, Surge and Mercor are recreating workplace data (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49343559). SimpleClosure's asset report lists 'manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services, logistics' as scarce-data buyers (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/what-your-assets-are-worth/). Its H1 2026 report shows its funnel is startups (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/state-of-shutdowns-h1-2026/). The main risk is privacy backlash. HN commenters doubt the de-identification ('I'm skeptical it'll be wiped correctly'), so the wedge is operational data with no consumer PII.
first_30_days: Week 1: pick two verticals, for example machine shops and freight brokerage. Book 20 calls with business brokers and CPAs who handle closures. Weeks 2-3: sign 3 exclusive listing agreements on a free data-asset scan. Line up 5 buyer LOIs from vertical-AI startups building quoting or dispatch agents. Week 4: complete one appraisal, get a privacy-counsel template for rights review, and run the first sealed-bid process.

title: Care-Home Trigger Desk: Evacuate, Shelter, Cool
one_liner: Automatic, pre-contracted action triggers that move older residents before fire, flood or heat-driven power loss becomes lethal.
customer: Multi-site senior living, assisted living and nursing operators in wildfire, coastal and heat-prone states, and their liability insurers.
problem: Older adults dominate heat, fire and hurricane deaths. Federal emergency-preparedness rules require plans but not pre-committed execution: buses, generator fuel, receiving-facility agreements and staff call-ins. Loss of power in heat kills.
solution: A facility-specific trigger sheet tied to near-real-time satellite fire detection, fire-spread modeling, AI weather ensembles and grid outage alerts. It launches staged actions: pre-contracted transport with SLAs, receiving-facility agreements, generator fuel top-ups and cooling-room setup, with an audit trail and drill simulations. Sold per bed per month.
why_now: Near-real-time satellite fire detection is getting funded and commercial (Satellites on Fire raised $2.7M), AI forecasting is cheap, and the summer 2026 heat set off demand for concrete heat plans.
revenue_model: $8-20 per bed per month, transport contract margin and insurer premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not information but pre-committed execution. Care homes have a legal duty and insurer pressure to buy it.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 operators in California and Colorado, build trigger sheets for 20 facilities, and sign transport partners.

title: Insider-Trading Watchdog for Entertainment Announcements
one_liner: Sportradar-style integrity monitoring for game publishers, studios and awards bodies whose announcements and results now trade as prediction-market contracts.
customer: Legal and compliance teams at game publishers, film and TV studios, awards bodies, esports leagues and streamers. Prediction-market exchanges are a secondary buyer.
problem: Kalshi valuation went from about $11B to $22B between Dec 2025 and May 2026, and entertainment and awards are already about 11% of activity. Employees, agencies, vendors and journalists under embargo hold non-public information that now has a price. No one monitors it, and sports leagues already pay for integrity services that entertainment lacks.
solution: Map every listed contract on Kalshi, Polymarket and other venues to the client's titles, awards and announcements. Detect abnormal volume and price moves ahead of reveals, and deliver incident packets for counsel. Add embargo-tier employee policy and training, and give exchanges a restricted-list API.
why_now: Prediction markets are expanding beyond sports despite state fights, and regulators will demand integrity partners as entertainment contracts multiply.
revenue_model: $2-10k per month subscriptions for IP owners, exchange-side API fees, and forensic investigations at project rates.
non_obvious_insight: Publishers think prediction markets are a gambling issue for someone else. For the first time, their 5,000 employees and 300 vendors hold embargoed information worth money. Sports solved this with third-party integrity vendors, and entertainment has none.
first_30_days: Build a tracker of all entertainment and gaming contracts across major venues. Publish a report on volume spikes before announcements. Contact compliance heads at 10 publishers and awards bodies, and sell one 3-month pilot at $5k per month.

title: Water Due Diligence for Small-Business Acquisitions
one_liner: A 5-day, fixed-price water-risk report for buyers, lenders and brokers of car washes, farms, RV parks, breweries and other water-dependent small businesses, plus a sell-side 'water-ready' file.
customer: Independent searchers and SBA buyers, business brokers and SBA lenders on $500k-$10M deals in water-dependent SMBs: car washes, farms, orchards and vineyards, RV parks and campgrounds, breweries and distilleries, nurseries, laundromats, ice and bottled-water plants, mobile-home parks.
problem: The Boomer sale wave meets drought. The value of these businesses rests on a tap, a well or a priority date that nobody puts in the sale memo. Phase I environmental assessments do not cover water rights, capacity, curtailment or PFAS and nitrate exposure. Buyers are first-timers with no diligence infrastructure. Search-fund capital targets $5-50M, and sub-$1M cash-flow businesses have no comparable formal capital.
solution: A 10-page report covering the legal water source and priority date, well permit and yield history, utility will-serve letter, capacity and moratoria, tap and system development fees, discharge and pretreatment permits, source-water quality against 2027 PFAS monitoring and nitrate, drought-surcharge exposure, a curtailment scenario under the Colorado River framework or state freezes, and an EBITDA-at-risk and price-adjustment table. A contract hydrogeologist reviews and LLMs assist with records pulls. Sell-side version: a $900 'water-ready' file that defends price.
why_now: From 2026-07-04 an SBA 7(a) loan can be combined with a 504 loan for up to $10M, so more real-estate-heavy deals will close. The Colorado River decision (Aug 2026) and Texas's Aug 3 grid freeze show that water and utility access can now stop a business. PFAS initial monitoring lands in 2027. 49.6% of the US is in drought. First-time buyers have no template for any of it.
revenue_model: $1,800-$3,500 per buy-side report. $900 per sell-side file. $299/mo broker pre-screen subscription. Bulk per-deal rate for SBA lenders. Referral fees from acquisition attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: Drought risk in a water-tied business is binary, not gradual. One curtailment or moratorium takes terminal value near zero, yet brokers, lenders and CPAs price it at zero. Whoever can put a number on the tap gets paid by buyers (walk away or reprice) and by sellers (defend the price). Once one bank asks for it, it becomes a checkbox for every SBA deal in the region.
first_30_days: Pick two states. Contract a hydrogeologist or water attorney for the review step. Go to 10 business brokers who specialize in car washes, farms and RV parks and offer 5 free reports on live listings. Ask two SBA lender loan officers to trial it. Convert 3 to paid at $2,500 by day 60.

title: Solar Defection Radar for African Utilities
one_liner: Africa's invisible solar and battery boom leaves utilities, banks and insurers blind, so measure it district by district.
customer: African distribution utilities and regulators, development finance institutions, commercial banks and insurers.
problem: Africa installs 17 GW in 2026 (+45%), 75% of it distributed. Ember's estimates are 2x official figures, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Utilities cannot see which paying customers are leaving, and lenders cannot price the assets.
solution: Estimate installed solar and battery stock per district from customs and import data, rooftop detection in satellite imagery and installer sales data. The wedge is a quarterly district-level report for Nigeria or Kenya, sold to one utility and one DFI.
why_now: Chinese exports hit records and batteries now outsell panels in import dollars. Ember's 'invisible boom' finding is public but nobody has productised it.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per institution, plus bespoke studies for DFIs.
non_obvious_insight: When self-generation outruns official statistics, the first credible dataset becomes the reference for tariffs, credit and insurance pricing.
first_30_days: Combine public Chinese export data, Ember figures and roof imagery for Lagos and Kano. Give a free sample to three utilities and one DFI.

title: Hour-Meter Forensics for Used Farm Equipment
one_liner: An independent inspection and identity report for used tractors and combines that cross-checks engine-hour logs across ECUs, serial numbers and liens to catch rolled-back hours and phantom sellers.
customer: Used-equipment dealers and auction houses, equipment-finance lenders and Farm Credit associations, and farmers buying $100K-800K machines on classifieds and marketplaces.
problem: Used machine value is driven by hours. Tools that roll back hour meters and ECU logs are openly sold, and buyers wire deposits to fake sellers. Lien and ownership checks are patchy. Row crops are projected to lose money for a fourth straight year and farm bankruptcies are up 19%, so lenders care about collateral and farmers buy used. Historically independent shops could not read OEM diagnostics, so no neutral party could verify a machine's history.
solution: Mobile mechanics with OEM-capable diagnostic tools pull hour counts from every module (engine, transmission, monitor, telematics) and compare them, review calibration and replacement logs, and flag mismatches. An identity module checks the serial against photos, runs a UCC lien search and does seller KYC, with escrow released on inspection. Output is a signed 'Hours Verified' certificate, later an API for lenders and auction platforms.
why_now: Deere's $99M settlement obliges it to open its diagnostic and repair tools for 10 years, creating independent access to the machine's real history for the first time. Repair restrictions cost farmers about $4.2B a year. Squeezed farm incomes push demand toward used machines, and leaked ID data feeds synthetic seller identities.
revenue_model: $195-495 per inspection paid by buyer or lender, $99 per lot from auction houses, a 0.5-1% escrow fee, and per-collateral fees from lenders for portfolio audits.
non_obvious_insight: Right-to-repair created a security market. Once independent shops can read what a machine really did, its history becomes a verifiable identity, a Carfax-like asset that OEM dealers, who profit from service and trade-ins, are structurally reluctant to publish. Whoever publishes trusted hours first owns the data asset.
first_30_days: Hire two ag mechanics who already own diagnostic tools. Offer a $150 'Hours Check' at three auction houses and five independent dealers during fall auction season. Publish the discrepancy rate as a case study. Then pitch equipment-finance lenders and Farm Credit associations a free 30-machine collateral audit.

title: The 4 A.M. Ride Guild
one_liner: A dispatch network of night-owl local drivers, paid per ride by hospitals and jails, that gets rural patients and released inmates home at hours when Uber and Medicaid rides do not exist.
customer: Critical access hospitals and their foundations, county jails, domestic violence shelters, crisis stabilization units, and Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans (through value-added benefits). Paid per ride, then by plan contract.
problem: A patient is discharged from a rural ER at 4am. She came by ambulance, her car is 30 miles away, and no taxi, Uber or Lyft exists. Medicaid non-emergency transport needs 24-48 hours notice and does not cover ER discharge. So she sits in the waiting room, a nurse drives her home (against policy), a relative is woken up, or the hospital admits her to observation for 'social reasons', which costs thousands. Jails release people at midnight with no ride, and domestic violence shelters have the same problem in reverse.
solution: A dispatch line (an SMS and phone flow with a human on call, then an app) that promises a driver within 30 minutes anywhere in a county between 10pm and 8am. Supply comes from people who are awake anyway: workers finishing third shift at plants, retired EMTs, volunteer firefighters and off-duty deputies. Riders can be dropped at a hospital, home or shelter, with documented handoff for CMS discharge planning. Add wheelchair-capable vehicles later. Insurance is hired and non-owned auto coverage, and drivers are background checked.
why_now: Rural hospitals are under pressure from Medicaid cuts and closing service lines, so avoiding costly observation stays and unsafe discharges matters more. Rural Health Transformation Program funds can pay for transport and access. Uber Health, Lyft and NEMT brokers are still thin at rural night hours, and the gap is a supply problem software alone cannot fix. Gig-style dispatch and background-check tooling is now cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: The hospital pays $85-110 per ride and the driver gets $55-65. A monthly minimum of $500-1,500 per facility guarantees driver availability, similar to a retainer. Later add Medicaid MCO and Medicare Advantage value-added benefit contracts. The ride log also supports the hospital's safe-discharge documentation.
non_obvious_insight: Nurses know that the ride is what actually gates a safe discharge at night, and that the hospital quietly pays for it in nurse gas money, observation admissions and ambulance runs. Transport startups assume demand is the hard part. In rural night hours supply is the hard part, and the winning move is recruiting people who are awake at 4am and paying them a guaranteed minimum. Hospital foundations, whose donors like 'getting Grandma home safe', are also a surprisingly easy first funder.
first_30_days: Sign one hospital and one sheriff's office for a pilot with a prepaid $1,000 retainer each. Recruit 15 drivers through third-shift plants, fire department Facebook groups and truck stops. Run dispatch manually via a Twilio group text with the founder on call. Get a hired-and-non-owned auto policy through a commercial broker and run background checks through a screening vendor. Track time to ride and observation stays avoided, and use those to pitch a second and third hospital.

title: SNAP-Ready Kits for Corner Stores
one_liner: A UPC-level 'variety counter' plus a pre-built wholesale fill kit that tells a convenience store exactly what to stock to keep SNAP authorization under USDA's new staple-food rule.
customer: Independent convenience stores, bodegas, small groceries and dollar-format stores that accept SNAP (USDA counts 269,217 authorized retailers, with small-format stores hit hardest). The store owner pays for the audit and kit. Secondary payers are the local cash-and-carry wholesalers and jobbers who earn incremental case sales, and city or state health departments that fund healthy-corner-store programs.
problem: USDA's final rule (effective July 7, 2026; implementation Nov 4, 2026) raises the stocking floor from 3 to 7 varieties in each of 4 staple categories (28 varieties), with 3 stocking units each (84 units) and perishables in 3 categories. The counting rules are counterintuitive: brown and white rice are one variety, all bread is one variety, and brands and flavors do not count. USDA's own analysis of 121,294 small-format stores found only 52% already stock enough dairy varieties and 63% enough protein, which implies roughly 58,000 stores short on dairy alone. Stores are assessed at reauthorization (every 5 years, about 54,000 stores a year) or at any time. Owners have no tool that tells them what to buy, and commenters said the rule is infeasible for small stores.
solution: An SMS and web tool. The owner uploads a POS export or photographs shelves. A classifier maps UPCs to USDA's variety groups, using the rule's Group 1 and Group 2 counting logic, and returns a gap list such as 'need 3 more dairy varieties and 2 more protein varieties, buy these SKUs'. A sold-through kit pre-negotiated with a local wholesaler uses the lowest-spoilage items that fit small refrigeration. The tool also produces a USDA evidence pack (dated photos, invoices, variety ledger) for reauthorization or a compliance review. A 'keep or drop SNAP' ROI calculator is built in, because most small stores earn little from SNAP.
why_now: USDA published the final rule on May 8, 2026 and the enforcement-ready implementation date is Nov 4, 2026, about five weeks out. The prior interim standard was only 3 varieties per category, so almost every small store has a gap to close. USDA also says it can assess any retailer at any time, and every store hits reauthorization within 5 years, so demand arrives as a rolling wave rather than a single date.
revenue_model: $79 one-time shelf audit, or free through wholesaler partners. Kit sold at wholesale plus a 10-15% margin, or a referral fee from the wholesaler. $29 per month monitoring with auto-reorder and evidence-pack refresh. Grant-funded 100-store packages ($500-1,500 per store) sold to health departments and food-access nonprofits. Anonymized gap data licensed to distributors.
non_obvious_insight: USDA admits it has no baseline data on how many stores fail, and its roughly $77M first-year cost estimate describes 'reviewing notice, guidance, and updating stock', which works out to a few hundred dollars per store. That looks far too low against stocking 28 varieties with perishables in tiny coolers, and commenters said so directly: 'refrigerated space is limited for perishable products... would lead to waste and higher operating costs' and 'stocking seven distinct grain varieties... is not feasible for small convenience stores'. Convenience stores are 44% of SNAP retailers but only 5% of redemptions and 76% of sanctions, so many owners will do the math and drop SNAP unless compliance is cheap and certain. The rule also leaves 'perishable' and 'stocking unit' undefined, which creates an interpretation gap that a shared variety ledger can fill. Evidence: final rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/08/2026-09137/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance and proposed rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/25/2025-18624/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance
first_30_days: Pick one metro with dense small-format stores. Sign one cash-and-carry wholesaler or jobber as the kit supplier. Encode the rule's variety-counting logic into a spreadsheet-based counter and walk 40 stores with a $79 audit, aiming for 15 paid audits and 5 kit orders. Publish a one-page 'what counts as a variety' guide and post it in grocer association WhatsApp and Facebook groups. Pitch the local health department a grant-funded 100-store pilot using the audit results as proof.

title: Remote Athletic Trainer Coverage for Rural Schools
one_liner: A subscription sideline triage line, protocol library and documentation service that stretches one licensed athletic trainer across many schools.
customer: Rural and small school districts, state athletic associations and school risk pools paying $6-20k per school per season.
problem: NATA-cited figures show about 41 percent of Kansas schools and 68 percent of Oklahoma schools lack an athletic trainer, only about a third of Arkansas schools have one, and Massachusetts does not require one (Boston Globe, September 28, 2026). Coaches make return-to-play calls and handle concussions, heat and cardiac emergencies ad hoc, and districts carry the liability.
solution: Licensed ATs run a game-time line where coaches call or video-chat for triage; ATs guide return-to-play, do next-day follow-ups, document per state concussion law, and supply emergency action plans and coach training. Optional phase two: AT review of clips from schools' existing AI cameras.
why_now: 2026 shortage coverage keeps escalating, legislatures are debating mandates, and schools already own cheap AI cameras and video-call tools.
revenue_model: $6-20k per school per season, district-wide contracts, risk-pool discounts, and per-event tournament coverage fees.
non_obvious_insight: Training more ATs will not fix this within five years; extending each AT's reach 5-10x will. School insurers and risk pools care about concussion litigation and will subsidize it, so it is sold as liability reduction rather than healthcare.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 part-time or retired ATs licensed in one state, pitch 10 districts on a 4-week football-season pilot at $2.5k, and pitch that state's school risk pool on co-funding.

title: Compute Boilers: Servers That Heat Buildings
one_liner: Install liquid-cooled inference servers in the boiler rooms of hotels, dorms, pools and laundries, sell the compute, and give the building cheap hot water.
customer: Hotels, university housing, municipal pools and YMCAs, multifamily buildings with central hot water, and laundries. They get cheaper heat. Inference providers buy the compute.
problem: Large AI sites wait years in interconnection queues, yet buildings already have continuous thermal loads, existing 3-phase service and unused headroom. Sub-MW loads avoid large-load studies. Owners face pressure to electrify hot water and building-emissions fines such as NYC's Local Law 97.
solution: Sealed 30-100 kW direct-to-chip liquid-cooled modules plumbed into building hot-water loops that capture most of the heat. The company owns and operates the hardware and sells GPU-hours to inference customers through a neocloud partner. The host gets heat at a discount to its gas or electric cost. First product: 20-40 kW pilots at about 10 hotels and pools in one metro.
why_now: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling is now standard, AI demand exceeds grid supply, small-model inference fits ordinary fiber, and UK pool and hot-water-cylinder server projects prove the model.
revenue_model: Compute revenue share, heat sold to hosts at 50-70% of their current fuel cost, and GPU-lender financing of the hardware.
non_obvious_insight: The grid is not short of electrons. It is short of interconnection at big sites. Sub-MW building sites already have service and a thermal sink, and heat reuse lowers hosting cost below any standalone data center, so the queue is bypassed.
first_30_days: Sign LOIs with five hospitality or pool operators in a state with cheap power and good fiber. Run heat-load audits. Spec a module with a liquid-cooling OEM. Get a GPU-lender term sheet. Deploy a 10 kW test unit at one site.

title: Birth Plan B for Maternity Deserts
one_liner: Carve the last three weeks of childbirth logistics out of the hospital: pre-booked lodging, ride dispatch, nurse triage and an emergency-delivery kit for mothers whose local labor ward closed.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans and state programs spending Rural Health Transformation money, rural employers and self-insured plans, and mothers directly ($349 to $699). Users: pregnant women in maternity-desert counties.
problem: At least 96 hospital labor-and-delivery units closed across 35 states between 2024 and early 2026, and in nearly 60% of affected counties it was the only birthing facility. About one in three US counties is a maternity-care desert, and more Medicaid cuts starting in 2027 are expected to close more units. Families improvise the final weeks: a 60 to 90 minute drive, no place to stay at 39 weeks, a partner who cannot leave work, and unplanned roadside births.
solution: A subscription from week 34. It includes choosing and pre-registering a receiving hospital, plus a contracted hotel or extended-stay room within 15 minutes of that hospital, for the 38 to 41 week window or triggered at first contractions. It adds on-call ride dispatch through a local non-emergency medical transport or taxi operator, with backup childcare and pet care. A 24/7 OB-nurse triage line (a telehealth partner) decides between go now and wait. The kit includes emergency-birth supplies and a 45-minute partner class coordinated with local EMS, and it ends with a return ride and first-week check-ins. No clinical license is needed because it wraps logistics around existing care.
why_now: CMS awarded the $50B Rural Health Transformation Program to all 50 states on December 29, 2025 (about $200M per state in year one). 35 state applications include maternal or child health, several include obstetric transport, and states face an October 30, 2026 deadline to obligate first-year awards. That makes subcontractors with a concrete pilot unusually welcome right now.
revenue_model: A per-member-per-pregnancy fee of roughly $300 to $900 from Medicaid managed-care plans as a value-added benefit, or a state RHTP subaward. Consumer self-pay of $349 to $699. Employer add-on for rural self-insured plans. Margin on lodging and rides.
non_obvious_insight: When a unit closes, the hospital's cost disappears and the family's cost explodes in the final three weeks. The fix is logistics (room blocks, dispatch, triage), which a non-clinical startup can assemble in weeks. Medicaid finances roughly four in ten US births and already pays for non-emergency transport, so the payer exists. The wedge is packaging this as a contractable benefit plans can add, with roadside-birth and ED-bypass metrics as proof.
first_30_days: Pick one closure county in the news and its receiving hospital 45 to 90 minutes away. Contract 6 discounted extended-stay rooms, one local transport operator and a telehealth OB-nurse line. Pilot with 20 mothers via the county health department, WIC and rural clinics, priced at cost or free. Log outcomes. Pitch two Medicaid plans' value-added-benefit teams and the state RHTP office with the pilot data and a one-page subaward proposal before the October 30 obligation deadline. In parallel, sell the consumer version through rural parenting groups, churches and doulas.

title: Purge-to-Spool Toll Recycler for Print Farms
one_liner: A mail-in service that turns multicolour purge waste and failed prints into laser-checked, guaranteed-diameter filament, so print farms get spools back without owning or babysitting a $1,200-$1,700 recycling rig.
customer: Print farms and Etsy print sellers running Bambu-style multicolour printers, maker spaces, schools and STEM programmes that produce kilograms of purge and failed prints monthly. Payer is the print-farm owner.
problem: Multicolour printing generates heavy purge waste, and existing recycling only pays in store credit. The DIY route (Creality's shredder plus filament maker) has diameter, jam and ROI risks that backers already worry about.
solution: Prepaid bins ship to the customer, who tosses in purge, supports and failed prints (same-polymer sorting only: PLA, PETG). The central facility shreds, dries, extrudes and spools with an inline laser micrometer, and returns a share of the weight as certified filament (for example a 1.75mm +/-0.03mm 'galaxy' random-colour spool). The remainder is sold as premium recycled filament. Customers see kg diverted and a certificate for 'green' Etsy claims.
why_now: Multicolour printing exploded (each Bambu Cube-style multicolour test can burn about 70 g of purge), and Creality's Filament Maker M1 and Shredder R1 hit its Indiegogo goal in 16 minutes and raised $6.8M from 5,320 backers, so waste is a felt problem. The first real-world tests show the DIY loop is not yet dependable, leaving a gap for a professional processor.
revenue_model: $3/kg intake fee (or pay-per-bin at $115 as Printerior's prepaid bins do), plus margin on selling recycled spools at $12-18/kg, plus a B2B subscription of $79-$199/mo for farms wanting monthly pickup and returns.
non_obvious_insight: Hobbyists backed a $649-$1,699 recycler, but the machine's own pre-production data shows why a service beats owning one. One reviewer measured filament diameter varying 1.78 mm to 1.58 mm across a single spool, and a complex print jammed at 97% recycled content. Creality itself recommends a 1:1 blend, and backers question ROI after electricity, failures and maintenance (https://makers101.com/creality-filament-maker-m1-shredder-r1-live-tracker/, raise figure of $6,816,733 from 5,320 backers; note that https://www.tcf.team/blog/q1-2026-crowdfunding-report reports a different $36M figure, so the exact total is uncertain, but demand is clear either way). Existing recyclers pay only points (Printerior: 280 points/kg redeemable for filament, and it requires sorted PLA/PLA+/PETG, https://printeriordesigns.com/pages/recycling), yet Printerior sells $114.99 prepaid bins, so people already pay to dispose responsibly. Nobody offers cash or spec-guaranteed spools back.
first_30_days: Buy a used 1.75mm extruder line, a shredder and a laser micrometer (about $6-10K) or rent time at a plastics co-op. Recruit 5 local print farms and 2 school maker labs as free pilots. Run 200 kg through, test diameter and print reliability in a 1:1 virgin blend, and photograph results. Then open pre-orders for prepaid bins ($115) and monthly pickup on the Bambu and Etsy-seller subreddits.
